alt: Two ways to consume a list from the front. With slicing, each pass takes the first item and builds a new list of the remaining items, copying them. With an index, the list stays where it is and the index moves one place right. The captions keep a running count of items copied by slicing, which adds up to n(n-1)/2, while the index version copies nothing.

steps.caption: `rest[0]` is 4, so `total` is 4. `rest[1:]` builds a new list and copies the other 4 items, so `copied` is 4. The index version reads `values[0]` in place and copies nothing.
`rest[0]` is 2, so `total` is 6. `rest[1:]` builds a new list and copies the other 3 items, so `copied` is 7. The index version reads `values[1]` in place and copies nothing.
`rest[0]` is 7, so `total` is 13. `rest[1:]` builds a new list and copies the other 2 items, so `copied` is 9. The index version reads `values[2]` in place and copies nothing.
`rest[0]` is 1, so `total` is 14. `rest[1:]` builds a new list and copies the other 1 item, so `copied` is 10. The index version reads `values[3]` in place and copies nothing.
`rest[0]` is 3, so `total` is 17. `rest[1:]` would be empty, nothing is copied, and `copied` stays 10. The index version reads `values[4]` in place.
Both versions reach a total of 17. Slicing copied 10 items along the way, which is 5 * 4 / 2, and the index version copied none. `rest` ended as an empty list.

Both versions reach a total of 9. Slicing copied 0 items along the way, which is 1 * 0 / 2, and the index version copied none. `rest` ended as an empty list.
